TDEE Calculator

A TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) calculator estimates the total number of calories you burn per day based on your Basal Metabolic Rate and physical activity level. It establishes your caloric maintenance baseline, providing the exact caloric targets needed for sustainable weight loss, weight maintenance, or muscle gain.

Formula and Calculation Method

Components of Total Daily Energy Expenditure:

TDEE = BMR + TEF (10%) + EAT (Exercise) + NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity)
Standard Multipliers: Sedentary (1.2) | Light (1.375) | Moderate (1.55) | Heavy (1.725) | Athlete (1.9)

Worked Example and Step-by-Step Calculation

Active Male Professional (32 yrs, 6 ft 0 in / 183 cm, 185 lbs / 84 kg, Lightly Active)
Input Values:
  • Age: 32
  • Height: 183 cm (6 ft 0 in)
  • Weight: 84 kg (185 lbs)
  • Sex: Male
  • Activity: Lightly Active (1.375x)

1. BMR = (10 × 84) + (6.25 × 183) - (5 × 32) + 5 = 840 + 1143.75 - 160 + 5 = 1,828.75 kcal

2. TDEE = 1,828.75 × 1.375 = 2,514.5 kcal / day

3. Maintenance Calories = 2,515 kcal/day

4. Fat Loss Target (-500 kcal) = 2,015 kcal/day

5. Muscle Building Target (+300 kcal) = 2,815 kcal/day

Result: BMR: 1,829 kcal/day | Maintenance TDEE: 2,515 kcal/day

How to Use the TDEE Calculator

  1. Enter your age, biological sex, height, and body weight.
  2. Select your physical activity level honestly based on your weekly routine.
  3. Optionally enter known body fat % to unlock the Katch-McArdle formula.
  4. Review your BMR, TDEE, and maintenance versus cut/bulk caloric thresholds.

Common Mistakes, Limitations & Practical Guidance

  • Fitness trackers frequently overestimate exercise calories burned by 20% to 40%.
  • Thyroid conditions, prior extreme dieting, and hormonal factors can affect actual metabolic expenditure.

Scientific Standards and Clinical Metabolic Guidelines

Physiological estimates generated by this application align with evidence-based standards published by the World Health Organization (WHO Technical Report Series 854), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM). Caloric requirements and basal metabolic rates are calculated using peer-reviewed anthropometric formulas, specifically the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, which clinical reviews validate as the most accurate predictor of resting metabolic expenditure in healthy adults.

Body composition analyses incorporate the U.S. Navy circumference method (NAVPERS 6110/5), providing body density estimates that correlate strongly with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans while eliminating equipment barriers for home users.

Three Practical Health and Fitness Application Scenarios

Scenario 1: Moderate Weight Management Protocol

An individual with a maintenance expenditure of 2,200 calories per day aims for sustainable body fat reduction. Establishing a moderate 400-calorie daily deficit results in a daily target of 1,800 calories. Over a 12-week cycle, this consistent deficit yields an accumulated deficit of 33,600 calories, producing approximately 9.6 pounds of fat loss while preserving metabolic rate.

Scenario 2: Athletic Recomposition and Macronutrient Target

A 75 kg resistance-trained athlete maintaining at 2,500 daily calories structures intake around lean tissue retention. Following International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) guidelines of 2.0 grams of protein per kilogram body weight, the athlete consumes 150 grams of protein (600 kcal), 70 grams of dietary fats (630 kcal), and 317 grams of carbohydrates (1,270 kcal).

Scenario 3: Sedentary to Active Lifestyle Progression

A sedentary office worker with a Basal Metabolic Rate of 1,600 kcal increases daily activity from sedentary (1.2 multiplier = 1,920 kcal TDEE) to moderately active (1.55 multiplier = 2,480 kcal TDEE) through 8,000 daily steps and three weekly workouts. This behavioral shift burns an extra 560 kcal daily without altering dietary intake.

Frequently Asked Questions About TDEE Calculator

How do you calculate daily water requirement by body weight?

A general baseline is 30 to 35 ml of water per kilogram of body weight (roughly half an ounce per pound), increased by 350 to 500 ml for every 30 minutes of vigorous physical activity.

What is the difference between BMR and TDEE?

BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the energy your body burns strictly at rest to keep essential organs functioning (heart, lungs, brain). TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is your BMR plus all additional energy burned through walking, working, digesting food, and exercising.

How do I choose the right activity multiplier?

Most desk workers who exercise 3 to 4 times a week are "Lightly Active" (1.375). Only people with physically demanding jobs (construction, mail delivery) or athletes training twice daily are "Very Active" (1.725+).

What is NEAT in energy expenditure?

NEAT stands for Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis. It represents all calories burned doing non-exercise movement: fidgeting, pacing, taking the stairs, typing, and yard work. NEAT accounts for significant differences in metabolism between individuals.

How often should I recalculate my TDEE?

Recalculate your TDEE every time you lose or gain 5 to 10 pounds (2 to 5 kg), as a smaller body requires fewer calories to operate and exercise.

How does this page relate to the Calorie and Macro Calculator?

This page focuses specifically on energy expenditure science and activity tier breakdowns. For detailed macronutrient gram targets (protein, carbs, fat splits), visit our Calorie and Macro Calculator.
